title: Piece activity

D0.outcome: Explains piece activity as the number of useful squares a piece reaches and the lines it controls, not how far forward it stands.

D1.outcome: Picks the more active of two placements of the same piece and points out the squares or lines that make it so.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled quiet positions, picks the move that most improves the worst-placed piece ahead of pawn pushes, in at least 7 of 10.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a one-feature change (a pawn that opens a line, a trade that frees a rook) shifts the activity balance, and explains why an advanced piece can be less active than a retreated one.

D4.outcome: In own games, names the worst-placed piece before quiet moves, and the choices are shown in the review log.

misconceptions: A piece further forward is more active.
Activity means making threats on every move.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K5 (mobility is the value of a piece); §7 row K5
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.7 (pawns that work vs pawns that merely need protection)
conditions: Mobility is the main criterion of a piece's worth in ordinary open or semi-open positions.
Central squares touch more of the board, so a piece there exerts more; the edge limits it.
A pawn move needs a purpose; a pawn that only needs protection is not working.
contrasts: A rook that wins the exchange but has no open file to enter gains no activity.
A knight on the rim after two moves has fewer squares than one on a central square.
A position decided by a forced tactic, where activity is moot.

soft_prereq_notes.OPN.PRINCIPLES.D1: development is the first form of activity
